parts.move: state which AC quantities instruments and mains ratings quote
parts.prompt: UK mains is described as 230 V, 50 Hz. State whether 230 V is the peak, peak-to-peak, or rms voltage, and give the peak-to-peak value.
scheme: 230 V is the rms value — the figure that gives the same heating effect as 230 V DC
Peak-to-peak = 2V₀ = 650 V
parts.answer: The 230 V mains figure is an rms value. The waveform actually swings to V₀ = √2×230 = 325 V each way, a peak-to-peak span of about 650 V.

parts.move: derive the 1/√2 factor from the time-average of sin²
parts.prompt: Explain, by considering the time average of sin²ωt over a cycle, why the rms value of a sinusoid is its peak divided by √2.
scheme: Instantaneous power in a resistor ∝ v² = V₀²sin²ωt
The mean of sin²ωt over a full cycle is ½
So mean power = V₀²/(2R), and equating to V_rms²/R gives V_rms = V₀/√2
parts.answer: Heating depends on the square of the instantaneous voltage. Over a cycle the mean of sin²ωt is ½, so the mean power is V₀²/2R. Setting V_rms²/R equal to that gives V_rms = V₀/√2 — the 0.707 factor comes entirely from averaging the square.

parts.move: explain how a reversing current still delivers net energy
parts.prompt: An alternating current reverses direction many times per second, yet a heater warms up steadily. Explain why the direction reversal does not cancel the energy transfer.
scheme: Power dissipated is P = i²R, and squaring removes the sign: both directions deliver positive power
The mean of i² over a cycle is I_rms², never zero
Energy accumulates regardless of which way the charge flows
parts.answer: The heating depends on i²R, and squaring makes every half-cycle positive — current in either direction warms the element. Averaging i² over the cycle gives I_rms², so energy flows continuously even though the net charge transferred is zero.

parts.move: read both amplitude and period from an oscilloscope trace to get peak and frequency
parts.prompt: An oscilloscope displays a sinusoid spanning 5.0 vertical divisions at 5 V per division, with one full cycle covering 4.0 horizontal divisions at 2 ms per division. Calculate the peak voltage, the rms voltage and the frequency.
scheme: The 5.0-division span is peak-to-peak: V₀ = 5.0 × 5/2 = 12.5 V
parts.answer: The vertical span is peak-to-peak, so V₀ = 25 V/2 = 12.5 V and V_rms = 12.5/√2 ≈ 8.8 V. One cycle takes 4.0×2 = 8.0 ms, giving f = 1/0.0080 = 125 Hz.

parts.move: derive resistive-load current from average power and Vrms, then report its waveform maximum
parts.prompt: A 230 V rms, 50 Hz supply drives a 1.0 kW heater. Calculate the rms current and the peak current.
scheme: The 50 Hz frequency does not enter the calculation
parts.answer: I_rms = P/V = 1000/230 = 4.3 A. The peak current is I₀ = √2×4.35 ≈ 6.2 A. Frequency is irrelevant here — the rms-to-peak relation alone sets the waveform extremes.

parts.move: reject the reasoning that AC averages to zero so delivers nothing
parts.prompt: A student argues that because the mean of an alternating current over a cycle is zero, an AC heater receives no net energy. Explain the error.
scheme: The plain mean of the signed current is zero, but power tracks i², not i
The mean of i² is I_rms² > 0, so the delivered energy is positive
parts.answer: It is true the signed current averages to zero, but heating follows i²R, which is positive in both half-cycles. The mean-square is what matters, and it equals I_rms² — not the square of the mean current, which is zero.

parts.move: transfer rms reasoning to choosing a fuse from a peak specification
parts.prompt: A heater is rated 3.0 kW at 230 V rms. A data sheet notes the supply reaches 325 V peak. Using rms values, determine the current the fuse must carry continuously, and choose the smallest standard fuse from 3 A, 5 A and 13 A.
scheme: The 325 V peak is a red herring for fuse rating: fuses respond to the heating effect, i.e. rms
13 A fuse (it must carry 13.0 A continuously)
parts.answer: The fuse sees the rms heating effect: I = 3000/230 = 13.0 A, so a 13 A fuse is required. The 325 V peak does not set the rating precisely because fuses respond to i²R heating, which is what rms encodes.

parts.move: transfer the rms definition to compare DC and AC supplies for the same lamp brightness
parts.prompt: A lamp glows identically when run from a 12 V DC supply and from an AC supply. State the AC rms voltage, then calculate the AC peak voltage it must withstand.
scheme: Equal brightness means equal mean power, so V_rms(AC) = 12 V
The filament must tolerate 17 V insulation-wise even though the effective voltage is 12 V
parts.answer: Identical brightness means identical mean power, so the AC rms voltage is also 12 V. The AC supply peaks at √2×12 ≈ 17 V — a reminder that components must survive the peak, not just the rms rating.

parts.move: combine rms power with the resistance-temperature dependence of a filament
parts.prompt: A tungsten filament has resistance 30 Ω at room temperature and 380 Ω at operating temperature. It runs from 230 V rms. Compare the rms current at switch-on with its steady operating current, and explain why fuses tolerate the switch-on surge briefly.
scheme: Switch-on current (cold): I = 230/30 = 7.7 A
Operating current (hot): I = 230/380 = 0.61 A
The surge is about 12.6 times the steady current, because tungsten's resistance rises steeply with temperature
Fuses are thermal devices with slow response; the momentary i²R heating does not reach the melting point in the brief surge
parts.answer: Cold, the filament draws 230/30 = 7.7 A; hot, only 230/380 = 0.61 A — a 12-fold inrush as tungsten resistance climbs with temperature. The fuse survives because it melts by sustained heating: the short-lived surge warms it only briefly before the filament resistance rises and the current collapses to normal.

parts.move: combine peak reading, rms conversion and power with a stated measurement uncertainty
parts.prompt: An oscilloscope's vertical calibration is stated as 2.0 V per division ± 5%. A sinusoid spans exactly 7.0 divisions. Calculate the rms voltage and the mean power in a 100 Ω resistor, and propagate the calibration uncertainty into the power.
scheme: Voltage uncertainty ±5% → power uncertainty ±10% (power ∝ V²)
parts.answer: V₀ = 7 divisions × 2 V/div ÷ 2 = 7.0 V, so V_rms = 7.0/√2 = 4.95 V and P = V_rms²/R = 0.245 W. Because power scales as V², the ±5% calibration error doubles to ±10% in power: P = 0.25 ± 0.02 W.
